description: This late 17th-century processional standard, known as an “‘Alam,” originates from the Safavid dynasty of Iran and is crafted from gilded brass with intricate openwork decoration. The standard is adorned with inscriptions in Nasta'liq and Thuluth script, featuring Arabic text along its shaft up to the join with the body. These inscriptions honor the Fourteen Immaculate Ones of Shi'a Islam, including the Prophet Muhammad, his daughter Fatima, and the Twelve Imams, despite the notable absence of the 12th Imam's name. At the pinnacle of the standard, a roundel bears the invocation "God is mighty," followed by inscriptions naming figures integral to Shi'a beliefs, such as Imam 'Ali and Bibi Fatima, and concluding with the invocation “Oh ‘Ali” in the largest roundel. These elements highlight the ‘Alam’s symbolic role in religious processions, showcasing its spiritual and cultural significance within the Shi'a community.

This Roman Provincial coin, crafted from alloy and produced between 253-268 CE, is indicative of the artistic and monetary practices of its time. It prominently features a crude depiction of a laureate, possibly draped and cuirassed bust of Emperor Gallienus from a rear perspective. The reverse side of the coin is adorned with the image of a triumphal arch, distinguished by three portals and windows positioned above the two side entrances. Latin inscriptions are present on both sides, though they suffer from partial obscurity and garbling, with some signs hinting at possible retrograde rendering. This artifact was unearthed in the Balkans, as suggested by related materials, illustrating the extensive reach of Roman coinage across the empire. Gallienus, an influential figure of the era, is notably named and portrayed on the coin, thereby anchoring it in the rich historical tapestry of the Roman Empire.

This Roman Imperial silver-plated coin, originating from the mid-1st century CE, exemplifies an ancient forgery, using a copper alloy core. The obverse showcases the laureate head of Emperor Claudius I facing right, with a Latin inscription: "[TI CLAVD] CAESAR AVG P M TR P X IMP P P." The reverse depicts a triumphal arch, intricately inscribed and crowned with an equestrian statue positioned to the left, flanked by two trophies, and bearing the Latin phrase "DE BRITANN." Not only does the coin reflect Claudius I's reign, but it may also allude to Pax (the personification of peace). This artifact was discovered in the Wortham Hoard, also known as the North Suffolk Forger's Hoard, providing a glimpse into ancient counterfeiting practices within the Roman Empire.

This Roman Imperial gold coin, dating from 294-305 CE, prominently features the laureate head of Galerius on the obverse side. The reverse depicts a campgate with its door open and three forward turrets, flanked by two smaller turrets between two towers. Latin inscriptions decorate both sides; the obverse bears "MAXIMIANVS CAES," indicating the period of Galerius as Caesar, while the reverse reads "VIRTVS MILITVM," celebrating the valor of soldiers. Additionally, the exergue displays the mint mark "PR," signifying its origin in Rome. Crafted from gold, this coin exemplifies the artistic and symbolic expressions of the Roman Imperial era. It was uncovered as part of the Beaurains hoard near Arras, France, contributing to our understanding of Roman monetary practices and Galerius' reign.

This Roman Imperial copper alloy coin, dating approximately to 317-318 CE, prominently displays a laureate, draped, and cuirassed bust of Constantine II, depicted facing right. The reverse side features a fort gateway with a star positioned above it. Latin inscriptions are present on both the obverse, reading "D N FL CL CONSTANTINVS NOB C," highlighting Constantine II's title as Caesar, and on the reverse reading "PROVIDENTIAE CAESS," emphasizing the providence of the Caesars, accompanied by a mintmark in the exergue denoted as "●MHTЄ[●]." This artifact exemplifies the numismatic artistry and imperial iconography of the period. The coin was unearthed as part of the Ibberton Hoard in Dorset, providing a tangible connection to the economic and cultural exchanges within the Roman Empire.

This Roman Imperial copper alloy coin, dating to 327-328 CE, bears the laureate head of Emperor Constantine the Great facing right on the obverse. The reverse depicts a camp gate flanked by two turrets, devoid of doors, with a star positioned above, indicative of varying stone layers depicted in the architecture. Latin inscriptions grace both sides: "CONSTANTINVS AVG" on the obverse, affirming Constantine's imperial status, and "PROVIDEN-TIAE AVGG" on the reverse, underscoring the providence of the emperors. Additionally, a mint mark in the form of a wreath surrounding "// SMALA" is present on the reverse. This coin, reflective of the iconography and minting practices under Constantine's reign, was unearthed at Antinoupolis, providing insights into the dissemination of currency and imperial imagery across the Roman Empire.

This Roman Imperial silver coin, minted in 307 CE, features a distinguished laureate bust of Emperor Constantine the Great, with the upper part of his cuirass visible, symbolizing his military prowess. The reverse side of the coin depicts a fort gateway, an architectural motif that reflects the strategic and martial themes prevalent during his reign. Latin inscriptions adorn the coin; on the obverse, it reads "IMP CONSTANTINVS AVG," while the reverse side bears "VIRTVS MILITVM," underscoring the valor of the army, accompanied by the mint signature "TR" for Trier in the exergue. Excavated from the Beaurains hoard near Arras, France, this artifact offers a glimpse into the monetary circulation and imperial iconography of Constantine's era.

This Roman Imperial silver coin, minted between 101-102 CE, prominently displays the head of Emperor Trajan, laureate and facing right, on the obverse. The reverse is adorned with a statue of Hercules, depicted naked and wearing a lion-skin on his head, standing frontally on a low base. Hercules is shown holding a club in his right hand with a lion-skin draped over his left arm, reflecting the classical reverence for mythological figures. The coin bears Latin inscriptions on both sides: the obverse reads "IMP CAES NERVA TRAIAN AVG GERM," while the reverse is inscribed with "P M TR P COS IIII P P." This artifact embodies the Roman Imperial era's artistic and cultural interplay between emperors and deified heroes. The coin was unearthed at Silchester as part of the Silchester hoard, offering a glimpse into the monetary history and archaeological context of Roman Britain.

This silver alloy coin, dating from approximately 200 to 160 BC during the Mauryan period, offers a glimpse into the numismatic art of ancient India. The obverse intricately features overlapping, separately punched motifs, including three standing figures, a square with three branches, and a depiction of an elephant standing to the right, accompanied by a four-legged insect below. The reverse presents traces of a circle nestled between two crescents, flanked by fish-like symbols, known collectively as the 'Taxila' mark, indicating its possible origins and trade associations in the region. Crafted using a punched technique, the coin's iconography reflects the cultural symbolism of the era, emphasizing elements like the sun, moon, and fauna. This artifact was found in Kabul and possibly Begram, underscoring the dynamic exchange of goods and artistic ideas across the Indian subcontinent and beyond during the Mauryan Empire.

This Mauryan silver alloy coin, dating from circa 269-187 BCE, originates from the heart of the ancient Indian empire and bears distinctive signs of its era. Adorned with five punchmarks, the coin features a prominent six-armed symbol alongside possible depictions of a tree, a square symbol, and a standard, although each is somewhat worn over time. Its reverse reveals traces of a mark, now largely faded. Crafted from a silver alloy, this coin not only served as currency but also as an embodiment of the symbols significant to the Mauryan culture. Discovered in Afghanistan, this artifact illustrates the expansive reach and influence of Mauryan trade and contact.

This Mauryan silver punchmark coin, approximately dated to 250 BC, exemplifies early Indian numismatic artistry with its elaborate design of five punches and three countermarks on the obverse, complemented by an additional countermark on the reverse. Reflecting the meticulous craft of the Mauryan Empire, the coin's distinctive markings likely served both decorative and functional purposes, embodying the evolving economic practices of ancient India during this era. Though the precise find spot remains unrecorded, such coins were pivotal in facilitating trade across the expansive Mauryan territory.

This silver alloy coin from the Mauryan culture, dated circa 200-150 BC, is a splendid example of ancient Indian numismatic art, discovered in Begram. The obverse is meticulously crafted with a series of overlapping punch-marks, featuring a sun, a six-armed symbol composed of alternating arrows and taurine heads encircling a central point, a three-arched hill accompanied by a crescent, a comb-shaped symbol within a square, and a depiction of a man standing on a plinth flanked by two taurine heads. The reverse continues the theme with a motif of four taurine heads surrounding a circle. Expertly created through the punching technique, this coin provides a rich tapestry of cultural and symbolic representations from the Mauryan era, reflecting the artistic and spiritual ideologies of the time.

This Mauryan cast alloy coin, dating approximately to 250 BCE, exemplifies the numismatic craftsmanship of ancient India. Made through a casting technique from an alloy, the coin reflects the economic and cultural milieu of the Mauryan Empire, one of the most significant and expansive empires of ancient India. Although inscriptions and specific iconographic subjects are absent, the coin's material and origin offer valuable insights into the trade practices and metallurgical technologies of the time. Its production during the Mauryan period marks it as a witness to one of the earliest and most influential phases of Indian history.

This Mauryan silver alloy coin, dating approximately from 269 to 187 BCE, is a rectangular artifact marked by wear and five punchmarks that reflect its ancient circulation. On the obverse, faint traces of a cockerel perched on an arched hill along with a tree enclosed by a railing are discernible. The reverse similarly features the remains of a cockerel on an arched hill motif. Minted during the Mauryan Empire, a pivotal period in Indian history known for its consolidation and expansion under emperors like Ashoka, this coin exemplifies the artistic and economic practices of the era. It was found in Begram, shedding light on the expansive trade networks that linked the Indian subcontinent with Central Asia.

This Mauryan silver coin, dating back to the 3rd century BCE, encapsulates the rich iconography of ancient India with five distinct punches on its surface. Among the symbols are a radiant sun, a six-armed motif, a sturdy bull, a majestic elephant, and a tree on a hill, each emblematic of various cultural and religious significances of the Mauryan era. Crafted from silver, this coin not only served as a medium of trade but also as a token of the expansive and sophisticated Mauryan civilization. Although the exact findspot remains unspecified, the coin's origin in India underscores its historical importance within the subcontinent's numismatic history.

This fragmentary silver punchmarked coin, originating from the Mauryan culture around the 3rd century BC, displays three of the original five punchmarks that adorned its surface. The visible symbols include a six-armed motif, a tree, and a caduceus, each carrying potential religious or symbolic significance within the Mauryan context. The coin's discovery in Begram offers a glimpse into the expansive trade networks and cultural exchanges within the ancient Indian subcontinent. With its intricate punchmark designs, this artifact provides valuable insights into the numismatic practices and symbolic representations of the Mauryan period.

This Mauryan-era silver punch-marked coin, dating back to the 3rd century BCE, exemplifies the numismatic practices of ancient India. Characteristic of its time, the coin bears symbols meticulously impressed into the metal, a distinguishing technique that identified its authenticity and origin. Issued during the reign of the Mauryan Empire, a pivotal period in Indian history, these coins played a crucial role in facilitating trade and commerce. While the specific findspot of this artifact remains unrecorded, its presence underscores the extensive reach and influence of Mauryan economic systems across the Indian subcontinent.

This Mauryan bronze coin, dating circa 200 BCE, encapsulates the ancient numismatic practices of India during a pivotal era of economic and cultural expansion. Despite the absence of inscriptions and defined subjects, the use of bronze material is indicative of the coinage standard of the Mauryan Empire, reflecting its widespread influence and robust trade networks. While specific details regarding its findspot remain undetermined, the coin's origin within the Indian subcontinent situates it within the broader historical narrative of the Mauryan dynasty's supremacy.

This Mauryan coin, produced circa 250 BCE, is a cast artifact crafted from an alloy, reflective of the early Indian empires' metallurgical practices. While the piece lacks inscriptions or detailed imagery, its creation during the Mauryan period underscores its cultural and historical significance, paralleling the empire's expansive reach and its adoption of coinage as a medium of economic exchange. Though the specific find spot remains undocumented, the coin's origins in India highlight its role within the context of Mauryan economic and social systems.

This copper alloy cast coin, dating to approximately the 2nd century BC, originates from the Mauryan period in India. The obverse side of the coin features intricate designs, including a standard, a cross-shaped tank, a swastika, and an elephant walking to the left. Its reverse displays a three-branched tree enclosed in a railing, a three-arched hill with a crescent, and an inverted sun and moon alongside a 'taurine' and standard motif. The coin bears inscriptions in both Prakrit and Greek; the obverse inscription, rendered in the Brahmi script, transliterates as "Rajane Agathuklayasa," while the Greek inscription on the reverse reads "ΒΑΣΙΛΕΩΣ ΑΓΑΘΟΚΛΕΟΥΣ," both translating to "of king Agathocles." This dual-language coin underscores the cultural exchanges between the Mauryan empire and the Hellenistic world, particularly Bactria under Agathocles. Found or acquired in Begram, the coin not only highlights the artistic and numismatic practices of the time but also serves as a testament to the interwoven histories and influences in ancient South Asia.

This silver coin, dating back to the 3rd century BCE, is a notable example of Mauryan numismatic art from ancient India. The coin is adorned with five distinct punchmarks featuring a sun, a six-armed symbol, a bull, a dog atop a hill, and three linked ovals, each serving as a testament to the symbolic richness of the period. Although lacking any inscriptions, the punchmarks convey the cultural and possibly economic messaging used during the Mauryan era. The coin's craftsmanship reflects the extensive reach and influence of the Mauryan Empire in ancient Indian history.

This Mauryan silver coin, dating back to the 3rd century BC, exemplifies the intricate craftsmanship characteristic of its era in ancient India. The coin is adorned with five distinct punchmarks, each symbolizing unique cultural motifs: the sun, a chakra, a bull, a dog on a hill, and a fish pond. These symbols are reflective of the prominent themes and beliefs in Mauryan society, such as spirituality, power, and the natural world. Crafted from silver, the coin offers a glimpse into the economic practices and artistic expression of the Mauryan period. Although its precise findspot remains unspecified, the coin's origin in India provides context for its circulation and usage during the height of the Mauryan Empire.

This Mauryan silver coin from the 3rd century BCE is distinguished by its quintet of punchmarks, comprising symbols such as a sun, a six-armed figure, a bull, a dog on a hill, and an elephant. Additionally, the coin bears two countermarks, indicative of revalidation or approval by subsequent authorities. These symbols provide a glimpse into the cultural and religious motifs of the Mauryan Empire, which spanned much of the Indian subcontinent. The coin's materiality, being silver, further emphasizes the economic and artistic practices of the era. Although the exact findspot remains unspecified, the production within India underlines its significance in the context of ancient Indian numismatics and trade.

This processional standard, known as an 'Alam, dates from approximately 1650-1700 and originates from the Safavid dynasty in the Persian region, modern-day Iran. Crafted from gilded and openwork brass, the 'Alam is notable for its intricate design and the rich symbolism it carries in a Shi'i religious parade. The shaft of the 'Alam is inscribed in Arabic using the elegant Nasta'liq and Thuluth scripts. The inscriptions, which span from the top of the 'Alam to where it joins with the body, include the phrase "God is great" in the top roundel, followed by the names of thirteen of the fourteen Immaculate Ones, omitting the 12th imam. The final roundel lists the names 'Ali and Allah. These inscriptions underscore the deep religious and cultural significance of the 'Alam, reflecting its role in Shi'i processional practices during the Safavid period.

This exquisite drawing, attributed to the artist Shafi` `Abbasi during the Safavid dynasty period of 1633-1674, depicts a delicate pomegranate branch adorned with two small bell-shaped flowers, alongside a flower characterized by almond-shaped petals and long, slender leaves. The harmonious composition, drawn in ink on paper, captures three insects hovering around the vegetation, while a rotund caterpillar traverses the ground below. The artwork is inscribed in Persian cursive in the upper left corner and along the lower right edge, with these inscriptions mirrored on the liner page opposite. Originally mounted horizontally, this single-page drawing is part of an album containing fifty-five drawings of flowers, plants, insects, and birds. The album, which was originally bound in leather with lacquered paintings of flowers on the covers, underwent restoration in 1942 as noted by Anthony Gardner. This restoration included replacing the leather binding with linen hinges and attaching the lacquer boards to new covers, while slightly trimming the folios. The drawing, reflective of Safavid artistic traditions, is a testament to the meticulous skill and aesthetic sensibility present during this era in Iran.

This Persian painting, produced between 1684-1685 (AH 1096), is a single-page artwork on an album folio, depicting a Qalander—a traveling Sufi spiritual figure—engaging a young devotee in conversation. The Qalander is portrayed bare-chested, adorned with necklaces of beads, and resting against a tree, his essential belongings—a hat, bowl, stick, and a reeded musical instrument—arranged before him. To the right, the devotee mirrors the mendicant's attire and gestures attentively towards the Sufi. This piece is executed in ink and opaque watercolor on paper, with an inscription in Persian positioned above the figures. Originally part of a larger album containing 44 pieces mostly showcasing Persian costumes and fauna, it is bound in brown leather with gold gilt decoration and lined with marbled paper inside the covers, highlighting its craftsmanship and cultural significance.

This exquisite single-page drawing, attributed to Shafi` `Abbasi and created during the Safavid dynasty between 1633-1674, beautifully captures the delicate elegance of nature. Rendered in ink on paper, it features a flowering, thorny branch of roses, complemented by a detached blossom lying beneath. The scene comes alive with three insects hovering around the flowers and a butterfly poised gracefully on a bud, while a pair of beetles crawls along the ground to the right. The artwork is inscribed in Persian cursive in the lower left corner, with the same inscription mirrored on the liner page opposite. Originally part of an album housing twenty-eight folios with fifty-five drawings of flora and fauna associated with Shafi` `Abbasi, the collection boasts leather-bound covers adorned with paintings of flowers. In 1942, conservation efforts by Anthony Gardner replaced the album's leather binding with linen hinges and attached the lacquer boards to new covers, slightly trimming the folios' lower edges. This illustration exemplifies the artistic finesse of the Persian section, evoking the rich cultural heritage of Iran during the period.

This exquisite single-page drawing from the Safavid dynasty, dating from 1633-1674, captures the elegance of a stem of carnations, complete with two buds and two fully open flowers. Rendered in ink on paper, the artwork is mounted in an album renowned for its meticulous depictions of flowers, plants, insects, and birds, attributed to the esteemed artist Shafi` `Abbasi. The album originally featured leather-bound covers with lacquered flower paintings, which were restored in 1942 when Anthony Gardner's memorandum chronicled the preservation process, including the replacement of the leather binding with linen hinges and attaching the lacquer boards to new covers. This drawing carries a Persian cursive inscription on the lower left edge, also repeated on the liner page opposite, and rests atop another drawing of a similar color, suggesting layered artistry. Housed in an album with twenty-eight folios, this piece reflects the rich artistic traditions of 17th-century Iran.

This early 17th-century Persian painting from Iran, rendered in ink, opaque watercolour, and gold on paper, portrays a seated woman in an evocative pose. She dons a thin, translucent robe that loosely drapes over her form, modestly covering her hair while leaving her breast exposed. Her downcast eyes convey introspection as she holds a small bowl gracefully in one hand while covering her breast with the other. The scene is adorned with strands of pearls accentuating her neck and wrist, set against a neutral background embellished with gold foliage, framed by a plain green border. Mounted on an album folio, this artwork is part of a larger collection featuring forty leaves of calligraphy and paintings, housed within lacquered covers displaying a central flower design and floral border. The album, bound in a concertina style, reads from right to left and includes an English inscription inside the front cover, "21 ff Aug 81875, EW," offering a glimpse into the manuscript's historical journey. This exquisite piece exemplifies Persian artistic traditions and contrasts themes of femininity, further noted by its "women/feminism" classification.

This exquisite piece from the Safavid dynasty, produced between 1633 and 1674, is a single-page horizontal drawing, mounted vertically, depicting two different types of flowers with a winged beetle crawling along the ground to the left. The left plant has a wilted blossom that has fallen to the center, while the right plant is characterized by small clustered flowers. Executed in ink on paper, this drawing is part of an album that originally contained twenty-eight folios with fifty-five drawings of flowers, plants, insects, and birds, attributed to Shafi` `Abbasi. The album was initially leather-bound with paintings of flowers on the front and back lacquered covers. A memorandum by Anthony Gardner from February 1942 describes the condition of the album before restoration measures replaced the leather binding with linen hinges and attached the lacquer boards to new covers, also noting that an eighth of an inch was trimmed from the folios' lower edges. The piece features Persian inscriptions in cursive running along the upper left edge, lower right corner, and lower edge center when the page is viewed horizontally, repetitively mirrored on a liner page opposite.

This exquisite single-page drawing from the Safavid dynasty, created between 1633 and 1674, depicts a finely detailed flower characterized by its small, overlapping petals and two leaves emerging from the base of the stem. Executed in ink on paper, the artwork is a testament to the Persian artistic tradition, associated with the renowned artist Shafi` `Abbasi. This drawing is part of an album containing twenty-eight folios with fifty-five illustrations of flowers, plants, insects, and birds. Notably, the album originally featured leather-bound, lacquered covers adorned with flower paintings, which were meticulously restored in 1942 by Anthony Gardner. Restoration efforts included replacing the leather binding with linen hinges, reattaching the lacquer boards to new covers, and trimming an eighth of an inch from the folios' lower edges. The drawing includes a Persian cursive inscription positioned at the lower edge left, mirroring another inscription on the opposite liner page. Although the specific findspot is unrecorded, the album resides as a distinguished piece within the Persian section, highlighting the rich cultural and artistic heritage of Iran.

This exquisite drawing, attributed to Shafi` `Abbasi and dating from the Safavid dynasty between 1633 and 1674, captures a delicate scene on a single-page horizontal sheet, mounted vertically within an album. Rendered in ink on paper, the artwork features an insect with two sets of wings gracefully hovering between two distinctive types of flowers. To the right, a symmetric plant displays a pair of open blossoms alongside its stem, while the left depicts a plant with a large blossom at the stem's end, accompanied by leaves and buds or wilted blossoms. The piece includes a Persian cursive inscription along the left lower edge, mirrored on a liner page opposite. The album, originally leather-bound with lacquered covers illustrating flowers, comprises twenty-eight folios containing fifty-five drawings of various flora and fauna. A memorandum by Anthony Gardner, dated February 1942, details the album's pre-restoration condition before replacing the leather binding with linen hinges and updating the lacquer boards. This carefully curated collection offers insight into the artistic and botanical interests during Iran's Safavid period.

This delicate single-page drawing from the Safavid dynasty, produced between 1633-1674 CE, captures the elegance of a tulip rendered with ink and wash on paper. The artwork is part of an album comprising twenty-eight folios with fifty-five drawings depicting flowers, plants, insects, and birds, attributed to the renowned artist Shafi` `Abbasi. The tulip is depicted against a void background, with an inscription in Persian cursive located in the lower left corner reading "lala shahri" or "tulip," which also appears on the liner page opposite. Originally bound in leather with lacquered covers featuring floral paintings, the album underwent restoration measures in February 1942, as noted in a memorandum by Anthony Gardner. These restorations replaced the leather binding with linen hinges and reattached the lacquered boards to new covers while trimming an eighth of an inch from the folios' lower edges. This exquisite piece exemplifies the intricate artistry of the Persian section and reflects the cultural richness of Iran during the Safavid period.

This exquisite artifact is a double portrait from a Mughal dynasty album folio, blending Persian artistry with Hindu cultural elements, fashioned in ink and opaque watercolor on paper. The folio consists of two contiguous paintings, showcasing rich cultural scenes. On the left, a worshipping woman performs puja at a shrine, accompanied by an attendant, an artistic depiction dating back to the 18th century. On the right, a circa 1590 painting illustrates a youth with frizzy black hair seated on a rock, expertly playing a rubab. His attire is opulent: white boots, blue trousers embellished with gold arabesques, a gold long cap, and a green jacket, cinched with a large orange and yellow sash. Natural elements enliven the scene, with a large butterfly poised to land on a flowering plant while dark clouds swirl above. The rubab player's armament—a sword and arrow sheath—rests beside him, conveying readiness and poise. A plain green border frames these vibrant compositions. The album, likely produced for a notable patron, features forty leaves of calligraphy and paintings, bound in an accordion-style with lacquered covers that boast a central flower design and floral border, speaking to the sophisticated aesthetic preferences of the era. This work is signed in Persian script by Muhammad Ja'far, and the inside front cover bears an English inscription with the date 21 August 1875, though its provenance and original findspot remain undisclosed, leaving a rich tapestry of artistic and cultural exchange open to interpretation.

This exquisite single-page drawing from the Safavid dynasty, dating between 1633 and 1674, depicts a large tulip accompanied by opening buds, fully blossomed flowers, and two symmetrically positioned insects. Executed in ink on paper, the composition is characterized by long, slender leaf blades growing from the base of the plant, contributing to the elegance of the artwork. Notable inscriptions in Persian, rendered in cursive, mark the lower left edge and an opposing liner page. Attributed to Shafi` `Abbasi, this drawing is part of an album originally containing fifty-five drawings that depict various flowers, plants, insects, and birds. The album, once leather-bound with lacquered floral paintings on its covers, underwent restoration in 1942. This involved replacing the leather binding with linen hinges and attaching newly lacquered boards after trimming the folios' edges slightly. This artifact serves as a testament to the artistic accomplishments and aesthetic sensibilities during the Safavid era in Iran.

This Roman Imperial silver coin, minted in 310 CE, features the laureate bust of Emperor Constantine the Great, with the upper part of his cuirass prominently visible. The reverse side of the coin depicts a fort gateway, an architectural motif signifying strength and protection. Inscribed in Latin, the obverse reads "IMP CONSTANTINVS AVG," affirming Constantine's status, while the reverse bears "VIRTVS MILITVM," extolling the virtues of the soldiers. Additionally, the exergue inscription "PTR" signifies the mint in Trier. This artifact, part of the Beaurains hoard, was excavated near Arras, France, providing valuable insights into the distribution of Roman currency and the veneration of imperial authority during Constantine's reign.

This Roman Imperial coin, dating from the mid-1st century CE, is an ancient forgery crafted from a copper alloy and skillfully silver-plated. The obverse features a laureate head of Emperor Claudius facing right, accompanied by the Latin inscription "TI CLAVD CAESAR AVG P M TR P X IMP P P." The reverse depicts a triumphal arch crowned with an equestrian statue flanked by two trophies, bearing the inscription "DE BRITANN," highlighting Claudius' conquest of Britain. This artifact offers a glimpse into the period's numismatic practices, specifically the occurrence of counterfeit coins. It was unearthed in Wortham, part of the North Suffolk Forger's hoard, shedding light on local economic activities and the circulation of imitation currency during this era within the Roman Empire.

This Roman Imperial silver coin, minted in 16 BCE, features the bare head of Emperor Augustus turned to the right on the obverse side. The reverse depicts a grand triumphal arch adorned with a quadriga, where Augustus is depicted standing and holding a laurel branch in his right hand and a sceptre in his left. Flanking this main arch, two smaller arches are each topped with an archer on the left and a figure possibly representing a slinger on the right. Although inscriptions in Latin are intended to embellish the reverse side, which includes the names S.P.Q.R IMP CAE and L. VINICIVS, they are not visible on this particular coin. This artifact reflects the political and cultural significance of Augustus's reign and the symbolic representation of Roman achievements. Discovered as part of the Forncett hoard, catalog number 362, it emphasizes the reach and influence of Roman coinage across the empire.

This Roman Imperial copper alloy coin, produced between 325-326 CE, prominently features the laureate bust of Crispus, depicted leftward, draped and cuirassed, on the obverse. The reverse side illustrates a camp gate with two turrets and no doors, detailed with varying numbers of stone layers and topped with a star. Latin inscriptions are artfully placed on both sides, with the obverse reading "CONSTAN-TINVS AVG" and the reverse "PROVIDEN-TIAE CAESS," coupled with the mintmark "SMALA." This coin serves as both a testament to the historical prominence of Crispus, son of Constantine the Great, and the military iconography prevalent within the Roman Empire. Excavated in Antinoupolis, the artifact offers invaluable insights into the numismatic and cultural practices of the period.

This Roman Imperial silver-plated copper alloy coin, forged in the mid-1st century CE, features the laureate head of Emperor Claudius facing right on the obverse side. The reverse showcases a triumphal arch, adorned with an equestrian statue of Tiberius between two trophies, providing a visual testament to the martial triumphs of the period. The coin bears Latin inscriptions on both sides; the obverse reads "TI CLAVD CAESAR AVG P M TR P VI IMP XI," while the reverse inscribes "DE BRITANN." This coin is an ancient forgery, reflecting both the economic practices and the challenges of monetary circulation during the Roman Empire. Unearthed at the Wortham hoard in North Suffolk, known as the North Suffolk Forger's hoard, this artifact offers insight into Roman numismatic history and the counterfeiting activities of the era.

This stoneware bowl rim sherd, originating from the Tang dynasty and dating between the mid to late 9th century, exemplifies the exquisite craftsmanship of Chinese ceramics. Wheel-made and adorned with a white glaze, it is further enhanced by vivid green splashes, a characteristic feature of Tang stoneware that highlights the era's aesthetic sensibilities. The artifact's origin is traced to Siraf, an archaeological site that offers a glimpse into the historical exchange and influence between the Tang dynasty and distant regions. Through its intricate glazing technique, this sherd represents the advanced ceramic practices of the period.

This artifact is a stoneware bowl rim sherd from the Tang dynasty, dating from the mid-8th to the early 10th century. Crafted using a wheel-made technique, the fragment is characterized by its green glaze, a distinctive feature of Tang ceramics that exemplifies the sophisticated glazing practices of the period. The artifact was discovered in Siraf, indicating the historical trade connections between China and regions along the Persian Gulf. This piece not only represents the material culture and artistic craftsmanship of the Tang dynasty but also underscores the extensive reach of Chinese ceramics during this era.

This artifact is a stoneware bowl body sherd from the Tang dynasty, dated to the mid-8th to early-10th century CE. Expertly wheel-made, this fragment is coated with a buff-colored slip, embellished with painted decoration, and finished with a clear glaze, demonstrating the sophisticated ceramic techniques of the period. Originating from China, it represents the artistic achievements of the Tang era, known for its advancements in ceramics. This exquisite single-page drawing, attributed to Shafi` `Abbasi and produced between 1633-1674 during the Safavid dynasty in Iran, is a masterful depiction of natural elegance. Originally, the album was leather-bound, featuring lacquered covers with floral paintings. A 1942 memorandum by Anthony Gardner documented pre-restoration conditions, which involved replacing the leather with linen hinges and attaching the lacquered panels to new covers, with folios slightly trimmed along the lower edges. This artwork reflects the intricate botanical studies and artistic sophistication that characterized the Persian cultural and artistic milieu of the Safavid era.

The album features lacquered covers embellished with a central flower design and a floral border, bound in a concertina style, typical of the intricate craftsmanship of Persian cultural artistry. An inscription inside the front cover in English, reading "21 ff Aug 81875, EW," adds a layer of historical intrigue. Although the find spot is not specified, this masterpiece hails from Iran, embodying the rich Persian heritage of its origin.

This Attic red-figured pottery acorn lekythos, dating from approximately 400-380 BCE, is a remarkable example of Classical Greek artistry, restored from multiple fragments. Its red-figure decoration vividly depicts the Festival of Adonis, with Eros poised on a ladder between women. On the left, a woman in three-quarter view sports added white flesh, adorned with jewelry rendered in raised clay, while her attire displays remnants of pink and lost color. At the center, Eros, marked by dark brown anatomical details and blue remnants on wings, stands on the ladder's second rung, holding a thymiaterion. A seated woman on the right, her attire hinting at traces of pink and green, gazes upon the scene. Many elements, including the jewelry, fillet, thymaterion, and ornamental knobs, were likely once gilded, adding a rich visual complexity to the scene. Discovered at a cemetery in Naukratis, an area known for hosting Greek communities in Egypt, this lekythos not only represents the skilled craft of its age but also reflects significant cultural and religious practices through its association with Eros and perhaps Adonis.
